title: The Relative Adjective ntj
short: ntj "who, which" introduces a relative clause: z ntj m pr "the man who is in the house"; jwtj "who is not" is its negative.
trouble: Students make ntj agree with the subject of its clause. It agrees with the noun it describes (ntt, ntjw).

blocks.html: Participles and relative forms make relative clauses out of verbs. When the clause has no suitable verb, for example "the man who is in the house", Egyptian uses a little adjective, ntj, made from the genitive n the way the nisbes of Nisbe Adjectives are made.

ntj "who, which" introduces a relative clause and agrees with the noun it describes: ntj (masculine), ntt (feminine), ntjw (plural). z ntj m pr "the man who is in the house"; zꜣt ntt m njwt "the daughter who is in the town". Its negative is jwtj "who … not": z jwtj zꜣ=f "a man who has no son".

ntj is a nisbe adjective: "the one belonging to …". Like every adjective it takes the gender and number of its noun. What follows it is a full clause, often an adverbial phrase (m pr) but also a whole sentence with its own subject: zꜣt ntt jt=s m pr "the daughter whose father is in the house", literally "the daughter who her father (is) in the house".

blocks.title: A clause with its own subject
blocks.q: Which form of ntj goes in zꜣt … jt=s m pr "the daughter whose father is in the house"?
steps: ntj agrees with the noun it describes, zꜣt, which is feminine.
The subject of the clause, jt=s "her father", is masculine, but that does not matter.
blocks.a: ntt: zꜣt ntt jt=s m pr.

blocks.title: The negative
steps: jwtjw: the plural of jwtj "who … not".

blocks.html: ntt also stands alone as a neuter, "that which", and after some prepositions it introduces a clause: ḥr-ntt "because". Those uses come up in reading; for now, learn the three forms and the rule of agreement.

Making ntj agree with the subject of its own clause. In zꜣt ntt jt=s m pr, students choose ntj because jt "father" is masculine. But ntj is an adjective describing zꜣt. Check: look to the left of ntj; the noun there sets its form.
ntj is used mostly after nouns that are definite ("the man"). After an indefinite noun ("a man") Egyptian often uses no ntj at all; see Clauses After Indefinite Nouns.
